title: 00 — Data Engineering & Databricks: Index
html:
00 — Data Engineering & Databricks: Index

The one idea: data engineering is the discipline of moving data from where it is produced to where it is useful, reliably, repeatedly and cheaply. Almost every tool in this set — Spark, Delta Lake, Databricks, orchestrators, quality checks — exists to make one of those four words true.

1. What this set covers

These notes explain data engineering the way a senior data engineer would explain it to a capable software engineer joining the team: the vocabulary, the processing models, how data is stored and modelled, how Spark actually executes work, what Databricks adds on top, and the patterns that separate a pipeline that runs from a pipeline you can trust.

It assumes you can already write code and SQL. It does not assume you have run a Spark job or designed a warehouse schema.

The existing chapter Python & Data Engineering covers Python itself, Polars and single-machine pipeline basics. This set picks up where that one stops: distributed processing, the lakehouse, and running data platforms in production.

2. Chapter map

# Chapter What you get from it
01 Data Engineering Foundations Roles, the data lifecycle, OLTP vs OLAP, data shapes, batch vs streaming, the modern data stack
02 Data Engineering Glossary A–Z reference of the terms you will hear every day
03 Data Processing Types Batch, micro-batch, streaming, ETL/ELT, CDC, load strategies, delivery guarantees, when to use which
04 Storage Formats and Layout Row vs columnar, Parquet and friends, Delta/Iceberg/Hudi, partitioning, clustering, small files
05 Data Modeling Kimball, fact and dimension design, SCD types, Data Vault, OBT, medallion layers
06 Apache Spark Driver/executors, lazy evaluation, shuffles, joins, AQE, skew, the Spark UI
07 Databricks Platform Compute, Unity Catalog, declarative pipelines, Auto Loader, Jobs, Asset Bundles, Azure setup
08 Delta Lake Transaction log, ACID on object storage, MERGE and SCD2, maintenance, Change Data Feed
09 Streaming Pipelines Structured Streaming, triggers, checkpoints, watermarks, state, foreachBatch
10 Orchestration, Quality and Governance Workflows/Airflow/ADF, data quality, contracts, observability, access control, GDPR
11 Pipeline Patterns and Practices Incremental loads, idempotency, backfills, CDC end to end, testing, CI/CD, cost and tuning

3. Suggested reading order

If you are new to the field: 01 → 02 (skim, then keep it open as a reference) → 03 → 04 → 05 → 06 → 08 → 07 → 09 → 10 → 11.

Reading Delta Lake (08) before the Databricks platform chapter (07) is deliberate for newcomers: the platform makes much more sense once you know what a Delta table actually is on disk.

If you already know SQL warehouses and want Databricks quickly: 04 → 06 → 07 → 08 → 11.

If you are about to build a streaming pipeline: 03 → 06 → 08 → 09 → 11.

If you own a platform and care about reliability and cost: 10 → 11 → 07.

Read it left to right: data is produced by systems that were never designed for analytics, ingested as faithfully as possible, refined in layers, and served to people and programs. Governance and orchestration are not boxes in the flow; they wrap around all of it.

5. How to use these notes

  • Every chapter opens with the one idea — if you remember nothing else, remember that sentence.
  • Chapters end with an Azure / .NET mapping (where the concept lives in the Microsoft stack) and a review checklist you can use to check your own understanding or to review a colleague's pipeline design.
  • Code samples are in SQL and PySpark. Where both are shown, they do the same thing, so you can pick whichever your team writes.
  • Product names change often in this space. Where Databricks has renamed a feature, both names are given, e.g. Delta Live Tables (now Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines).
